title: Lists & Dictionaries
description: Store ordered collections with lists and key/value pairs with dictionaries.

lesson.title: Lists & Dictionaries
lesson.summary: Python's two workhorse containers: ordered lists and keyed dictionaries.
lesson.body:
## Lists: ordered collections

A **list** holds items in order, inside square brackets:

```python
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
```

Access items by index (from 0) and update them in place — lists are *mutable*:

```python
fruits[0]            # "apple"
fruits[0] = "mango"  # lists can be changed
len(fruits)           # 3
```

Common list operations:

```python
fruits.append("kiwi")    # add to the end
fruits.insert(0, "pear")  # add at a position
fruits.remove("banana")   # remove by value
fruits.pop()               # remove & return the last item
"apple" in fruits          # membership test -> True/False
```

## Dictionaries: key/value pairs

A **dictionary** maps keys to values, inside curly braces:

```python
person = {"name": "Ada", "age": 30}
```

Look things up and update them by key:

```python
person["name"]          # "Ada"
person["age"] = 31       # update
person["city"] = "London" # add a new key
"email" in person        # False
```

Use `.get()` to avoid errors when a key might be missing:

```python
person.get("email")              # None (no error)
person.get("email", "unknown")  # "unknown" (default)
```

## When to use which

- Reach for a **list** when order matters and you mostly access items by position.
- Reach for a **dict** when you look things up by a meaningful key (a name, an id).

Both can hold any type of value, and they can be nested — a list of dicts is extremely common.

examples.title: Grow and shrink a list
examples.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana"]
fruits.append("cherry")
fruits.insert(0, "pear")
print(fruits)
last = fruits.pop()
print("removed:", last)
print("remaining:", fruits)

examples.title: Look things up in a dict
examples.description: Notice how .get() returns a default instead of crashing.

questions.explanation: Curly braces `{}` with key: value pairs create a dict. Square brackets make a list.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
nums = [10, 20, 30]
nums.append(40)
print(len(nums))
```
questions.explanation: append adds one item, so the list now has 4 elements.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
d = {"a": 1}
print(d.get("b", 0))
```
questions.explanation: Key "b" is missing, so .get returns the default 0 (no error).

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
fruits = ["apple", "banana"]
print("cherry" in fruits)
```
questions.explanation: "cherry" is not in the list, so the membership test is False.

questions.prompt: You want to store a phone book that maps names to numbers. Which is the better fit?
questions.explanation: Looking up by a meaningful key (a name) is exactly what dictionaries are for.

flashcards.back: `d["name"]` — or `d.get("name")` to avoid a KeyError if it's missing.
Yes. You can change, add, and remove items in place.
A bool — True if the item/key is present, False otherwise.

flashcards.front: List vs dict: which for lookup by meaningful key?
flashcards.back: A dictionary. Use a list when order/position matters.
